uncited: Depth to Distance Conversion transforms sampled depth values ($z_{vals}$) along a ray into segment lengths ($dists$) required for volume rendering integration.
It accounts for the viewing angle by scaling the depth differences with the cosine of the angle between the ray direction and the viewing direction.

This method is distinct from [Interpolation Schemes for Volume Rendering](817-interpolation-schemes-for-volume-rendering.md) as it focuses on metric length calculation rather than value estimation, and from [Sampling and Jittering](2516-sampling-and-jittering.md) as it operates on already sampled points.
- $cos\_angle$: Tensor of cosine values of the angle between the ray direction and the viewing direction, shape $(..., 1)$.
This results in a tensor of shape $(..., N-1)$.
Append a large value to represent the distance to the last segment (often used to ensure the last sample contributes fully or to handle boundary conditions).
The value $10^{10}$ is used as a proxy for infinity.
The appended value is expanded to match the batch dimensions.
- **Precision:** Ensure $z_{vals}$ and $cos\_angle$ are on the same device and have compatible dtypes to avoid runtime errors.
- **Boundary Conditions:** The last segment is approximated with a large value ($10^{10}$).
This assumes that the last sample is effectively at infinity or that the contribution of the last segment is negligible if the density is zero.
If the last sample is not at infinity, this approximation may introduce errors.
- **Cosine Angle:** If $cos\_angle$ is zero (ray perpendicular to view direction), all distances become zero, which may lead to division by zero or incorrect integration if not handled.
Computes segment distances between consecutive Normalized Device Coordinate (NDC) points.
It differs from the standard Depth to Distance method by using Euclidean distance in NDC space rather than depth differences.
Compute Euclidean distance: $dists = \text{norm}(ndc\_pts[:, 1:] - ndc\_pts[:, :-1], \text{dim}=-1)$.
Append large value and scale: $dists = \text{concat}(dists, 10^{10} \times cos\_angle)$, scaled by cosine.
- **When to choose:** Use when working with NDC space representations where Euclidean distance in NDC space is more appropriate than depth differences.
- **Time Complexity:** $O(N)$, where $N$ is the number of samples.
The operations are element-wise and involve simple arithmetic.
- **Memory Complexity:** $O(N)$ for storing the output distances.
- **Strengths:** Simple to implement, accounts for viewing angle, handles boundary conditions with a large value approximation.
- **When to use:** Standard volume rendering pipelines where depth samples are uniformly distributed in depth space.
- **When not to use:** When non-uniform sampling is used, or when the last segment needs precise distance calculation.
Originated in the context of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and volume rendering, where accurate segment distances are crucial for correct integration of radiance along rays.
The method is commonly used in implementations of NeRF and related techniques.
